name: Jyotiṣa (the science of the lights)
regions: Ujjayinī (the prime meridian of the siddhāntas)

tradition.text: revealed science of the seers: taught by Brahmā, Sūrya and the eighteen promulgators; the same science told anew in every age (SS 1.8–9)

scholarly.text: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa in the later first millennium BCE; horoscopy from the early centuries CE; siddhānta astronomy from the 5th c. CE (Āryabhaṭa 499); continuous to the present

transmissions_received.what: the lunar mansions, the five-year yuga and time-reckoning for the sacrifice
transmissions_received.evidence: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa; the nakṣatra lists of the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas

transmissions_received.what: horoscopy with signs, houses and planetary rulers (scholarly account: of Hellenistic origin)
transmissions_received.evidence: Yavanajātaka; Greek-derived technical words in the Bṛhajjātaka (1.8, 1.17–18, 2.2–3); BS 2.14

transmissions_received.what: annual horoscopy, Arabic lots and aspect-yogas (scholarly account: from Perso-Arabic astrology)
transmissions_received.evidence: Tājika texts from the 13th c.; Nīlakaṇṭha 1587

transmissions_given.what: muhūrta rules, tithi decisions and the planetary sacrifice in the smṛtis and digests
site, house and temple rules and auspicious times (BS 52–57; MC vāstu-prakaraṇa)
calendrical astronomy taken up in the Kālacakra system (scholarly account)
later Jain horoscopy and Tājika authors (Hemaprabha)

distinctive_positions: Jyotiṣa is the eye of the Veda and stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas, because rites depend on times (VJ; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 41–42).
The science has three branches (skandha): gaṇita/siddhānta (computation), saṃhitā (omens and mundane matters) and horā (nativities) (BS 1.9; BPHS 1.2).
The birth chart reveals the ripening of good and bad karma earned in a former birth, as a lamp shows objects in darkness (BJ 1.3; LJ 1.3).
The planets are forms of Janārdana that give beings the fruits of their karma (BPHS 2.3); their wrath can be pacified by worship, gifts, mantra and fire-offering (YājñSm 1.295–308; BPHS 84).
Fate (daiva) is karma made in another birth; success needs fate and human effort together, like farming (Yogayātrā 1.3–4).
Time is twofold: the time that ends the worlds, and measurable time (SS 1.10).
Eclipses occur by the shadow of the earth and the body of the moon; Rāhu is present at the eclipse by Brahmā's boon and receives its offerings (BS 5.8–15).
A king or householder should act at a time when the planets are well placed (BS 103.59–60; Muhūrta Cintāmaṇi).
summary: Jyotiṣa, the Vedāṅga of the heavenly lights, began as the reckoning of times for the Vedic sacrifice (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa) and grew into three branches: mathematical astronomy (siddhānta), mundane astrology and omens (saṃhitā), and horoscopy (horā/jātaka), later also interrogation (praśna), electional timing (muhūrta) and the Indo-Persian Tājika. It teaches that the planets, signs and lunar mansions reveal — and as divine powers dispense — the fruits of past karma, and prescribes timing and pacificatory rites. It is a limb of the Veda rather than a path to liberation, though it names signs of renunciation and liberation in the chart.

name: The Kerala tradition of jyotiṣa

scholarly.text: Parahita system 683 CE; the Saṅgamagrāma school c. 1350–1650; Praśna Mārga 1649

distinctive_positions: Follows the Āryabhaṭa school (āryapakṣa) in astronomy, corrected by observation (Parahita, Dṛggaṇita).
Cultivates horā through Malayalam-country commentaries on the Bṛhajjātaka (Rudra's Vivaraṇa, Govinda Bhaṭṭatiri's Daśādhyāyī).
Developed an elaborate interrogation ritual (aṣṭamaṅgala-praśna; devaprāśna for temples) codified in the Praśna Mārga.
summary: The Kerala stream of jyotiṣa: astronomers of the Āryabhaṭa school (Haridatta's Parahita, Parameśvara's Dṛggaṇita, the Saṅgamagrāma lineage of Mādhava, Parameśvara, Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī and Jyeṣṭhadeva) and a strong horā and praśna tradition carried in Nambūtiri and Piṣāraṭi families, with the Praśna Mārga as its manual of interrogation and remedies.

name: Tājika (Indo-Persian annual and interrogational astrology)

scholarly.text: c. 13th c. CE onward; systematized by Nīlakaṇṭha 1587

distinctive_positions: The annual chart (varṣaphala) cast for the sun's return to its birth position.
Sixteen aspect-combinations with Perso-Arabic names (itthaśāla, īsarāpha, etc.).
Sensitive points called sahama and the progressed point muntha.
summary: Tājika is the branch of jyotiṣa that took over Perso-Arabic methods — annual revolutions, the sixteen Tājika yogas, sahamas and muntha — written in Sanskrit from the 13th century by Brahmin and Jain authors and standardized in Nīlakaṇṭha's Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī (1587). The name itself (tājika, 'Persian/Arab') marks the tradition's awareness of its foreign source.
notes: Family set to 'shared' because Jain authors (Hemaprabha) wrote Tājika texts. No separate lineage id exists for Perso-Arabic astrology (outside scope).

name: Nāḍī jyotiṣa (palm-leaf readings ascribed to the seers)

tradition.text: the seers (Agastya, Bhṛgu, Kauśika, Vasiṣṭha and others) wrote the leaves in ancient times, foreseeing each seeker

scholarly.text: surviving manuscripts and documented reading practice are late (mostly 19th–20th c.)

distinctive_positions: The tradition's claim: the seers foresaw every individual who would come to consult them and wrote their lives on palm leaves.
Leaves are located by thumb-impression classes and read aloud in Tamil verse, in chapters (kāṇḍa) including past-birth karma and remedies (śānti-parihāra).
summary: The nāḍī tradition claims palm-leaf manuscripts written by ancient seers that record the life, past births and remedies of the individual who comes to consult them. Recorded here as the tradition's claim; the documented practice and manuscripts are recent.

name: The Yavana school of horā

scholarly.text: Yavaneśvara's prose rendering 149/150 CE and Sphujidhvaja's verse version 269/270 CE (Pingree's reading; the dates are debated)

distinctive_positions: Horoscopy by signs, houses (kendra, paṇaphara, āpoklima), decans and planetary rulers.
Its views are quoted and sometimes rejected by Varāhamihira (BJ 7.1, 11.1, 12.1).
summary: The 'Yavanas' are the teachers of horā whom Varāhamihira cites and honours: 'the Yavanas are mlecchas, yet this science is well established among them, and they are honoured like seers' (BS 2.14). Their texts (the Yavanajātaka of Sphujidhvaja, Mīnarāja's Vṛddhayavanajātaka) were absorbed into mainstream horā.
